lessons.title: Angles and polygons
lessons.summary: Use the basic angle facts, the rules for parallel lines and the angle sums of triangles, quadrilaterals and polygons to find missing angles and give clear reasons for every step.
objectives: I can use the facts for angles on a straight line, around a point and vertically opposite angles.
I can identify alternate, corresponding and co-interior angles in parallel lines and use them with reasons.
I can find missing angles in triangles and quadrilaterals, including isosceles triangles and special quadrilaterals.
I can work out the sum of the interior angles of any polygon and use the fact that exterior angles add to 360°.
I can find the interior and exterior angles of a regular polygon, or the number of sides from one angle.

activities.title: The basic angle facts
activities.content:
## Four facts you will use constantly

Almost every angle question is built from a handful of facts. Learn the wording, because examiners give marks for **reasons** as well as answers.

| Fact | Wording to write |
|---|---|
| Angles on a straight line add up to 180° | *angles on a straight line* |
| Angles around a point add up to 360° | *angles at a point* |
| Vertically opposite angles are equal | *vertically opposite angles* |
| A right angle is 90° | *right angle* |

**Vertically opposite angles** appear where two straight lines cross. The picture looks like a letter X:

```
   a\  /b
     \/
     /\
   c/  \d
```

Here angle *a* = angle *d* and angle *b* = angle *c*. The angles are opposite each other **at the vertex** (the crossing point), which is where the name comes from. Also, *a* + *b* = 180° because together they sit on a straight line.

**A quick tip:** if a question shows several angles meeting at one point on a straight line, add up the ones you know, subtract from 180° and you have the missing one. If the angles go all the way round the point, subtract from 360° instead.

When the angles are given as expressions such as $2x + 10$, write an equation using the fact, then solve it.

activities.title: Worked example: angles around a point
activities.content:
**Question:** Four angles meet at a point. They are $2x$, $3x + 10$, $90°$ and $x + 20$. Find $x$ and each angle.

**Step 1 – choose the fact.** The angles go all the way round the point, so they add up to 360°.

**Step 2 – write the equation.**

$2x + (3x + 10) + 90 + (x + 20) = 360$

$6x + 120 = 360$

**Step 3 – solve.**

$6x = 240$, so $x = 40$.

**Step 4 – find each angle and check.**

- $2x = 80°$
- $3x + 10 = 130°$
- $90°$
- $x + 20 = 60°$

Check: $80 + 130 + 90 + 60 = 360$. Correct.

Always do the check at the end. It takes ten seconds and catches most slips.

question.text: Three angles lie together on a straight line. They are $4y$, $y + 15$ and $40°$. Work out the value of $y$.
question.hint: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. Write an equation and collect the $y$ terms.

activities.title: Angles in parallel lines
activities.content:
## Parallel lines and a transversal

When a straight line (called a **transversal**) crosses two **parallel** lines, it makes eight angles, but there are only ever two different sizes: an acute one and an obtuse one, and those two add up to 180°.

```
 ------/------   (top parallel line)
      /p  q
     /r  s
 ------/------   (bottom parallel line)
      /
```

There are three named pairs, each with a letter shape that helps you spot them:

- **Alternate angles are equal.** They sit on *opposite* sides of the transversal, between the parallel lines, making a **Z** shape (sometimes a back-to-front Z).
- **Corresponding angles are equal.** They are in the *same position* at each crossing, making an **F** shape (the F may be upside down or reversed).
- **Co-interior angles add up to 180°.** They are on the *same* side of the transversal, between the parallel lines, making a **C** or **U** shape. Some people call them allied angles.

The letter shapes are only a memory aid. In the exam you must write the proper name, for example "angle x = 54° because alternate angles are equal". Writing "Z angles" scores nothing for the reason.

Remember that the arrows on the lines are what tell you they are parallel. If there are no arrows you cannot use these rules.

activities.title: Worked example: reasons with parallel lines
activities.content:
**Question:** Two parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. At the top crossing, the angle above the top line and to the right of the transversal is 68°. Find the other angles at the bottom crossing, with reasons.

Label the bottom crossing angles as: *top-right* (above the bottom line, right of the transversal), *top-left*, *bottom-right* and *bottom-left*.

**Bottom crossing, top-right = 68°** because it is in the same position as the given angle: **corresponding angles are equal**.

**Bottom crossing, top-left = 112°** because it lies on a straight line with the 68°: **angles on a straight line add up to 180°**, and $180 - 68 = 112$.

**Bottom crossing, bottom-left = 68°** because it is **vertically opposite** the 68° at that crossing.

**Bottom crossing, bottom-right = 112°** because it is vertically opposite the 112°.

Notice how every angle is either 68° or 112°. That is always true for a single transversal: once you know one angle you can find all eight, and the only skill is naming the right reason.

question.text: Match each type of angle pair to the correct rule.
question.hint: Think of the letter shapes Z, F and C, and remember that only one of the parallel-line pairs adds up to 180°.
question.explanation: Alternate angles (Z shape) are equal. Corresponding angles (F shape) are equal. Co-interior angles (C shape) add up to 180°. Angles around a point add up to 360°.

pairs.right: Equal – found in a Z shape
Equal – found in an F shape
Add up to 180° – found in a C shape

activities.title: Triangles and quadrilaterals
activities.content:
## Angle sums

- The interior angles of a **triangle** add up to **180°**.
- The interior angles of a **quadrilateral** add up to **360°** (cut it along a diagonal and you get two triangles).

## Special triangles

| Triangle | What you know |
|---|---|
| Equilateral | all sides equal, all angles 60° |
| Isosceles | two equal sides, and the two **base angles** (opposite the equal sides) are equal |
| Right-angled | one angle is 90°, so the other two add up to 90° |

In an isosceles triangle the little dashes on the sides show which two are equal. The equal angles are the ones *not* between the two dashed sides.

## The exterior angle of a triangle

Extend one side of a triangle. The angle formed outside is the **exterior angle**, and it equals the **sum of the two interior angles on the opposite side** (the two angles not next to it). This is a handy shortcut that saves a step.

## Special quadrilaterals

- **Parallelogram**: opposite angles equal, neighbouring angles add to 180°.
- **Rhombus**: a parallelogram with four equal sides (same angle facts).
- **Kite**: one pair of opposite angles equal (the ones between the unequal sides).
- **Trapezium**: one pair of parallel sides, so the angles at each end of a non-parallel side are co-interior and add to 180°.

activities.title: Worked example: exterior angle and a kite
activities.content:
**Part A.** In triangle PQR, angle P = 47° and angle Q = 61°. Side QR is extended beyond R to a point S. Find the exterior angle PRS.

*Method 1 (two steps):* angle R = $180 - 47 - 61 = 72°$ (angles in a triangle). Then angle PRS = $180 - 72 = 108°$ (angles on a straight line).

*Method 2 (shortcut):* the exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles: $47 + 61 = 108°$.

Both give **108°**, and both are acceptable in an exam as long as you give the reason.

**Part B.** A kite has angles of 124° and 78° at the two ends of its line of symmetry. Find the other two angles.

The remaining two angles are the equal pair. Their total is $360 - 124 - 78 = 158°$, so each is $158 ÷ 2 = 79°$.

Check: $124 + 78 + 79 + 79 = 360$. Correct.

question.text: An isosceles triangle has an angle of 38° between its two equal sides. What is the size of each of the other two angles?
question.hint: The two base angles are equal and all three angles add up to 180°.
question.explanation: The two base angles share $180 - 38 = 142°$, so each is $142 ÷ 2 = 71°$.

options.feedback: That is the total of the two base angles, not one of them.
The equal angles are opposite the equal sides, not the angle between them.
You have subtracted 38 from 90, but the angles add to 180°, not 90°.

activities.title: Interior and exterior angles of polygons
activities.content:
## Any polygon

A polygon with $n$ sides can be split into $n - 2$ triangles by drawing diagonals from one vertex. Each triangle contributes 180°, so:

**Sum of interior angles = $(n - 2) × 180°$**

| Shape | Sides | Interior angle sum |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 180° |
| Quadrilateral | 4 | 360° |
| Pentagon | 5 | 540° |
| Hexagon | 6 | 720° |
| Octagon | 8 | 1080° |

An **exterior angle** is made by extending a side; it sits between the extension and the next side. At each vertex, interior + exterior = 180°. If you walk all the way round the shape you turn through one full turn, so:

**The exterior angles of any polygon add up to 360°.** This is true however many sides there are.

## Regular polygons

A **regular** polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal. That makes the exterior angles equal too, so:

- exterior angle = $360° ÷ n$
- interior angle = $180° -$ exterior angle
- number of sides $n = 360° ÷$ exterior angle

The exterior angle is the key. If a question gives you an interior angle, subtract it from 180° first to get the exterior angle, then divide into 360°.

For an irregular polygon you cannot use these regular-polygon shortcuts; instead use the interior sum $(n - 2) × 180°$ and form an equation.

activities.title: Worked example: a regular nonagon
activities.content:
**Question:** A regular nonagon has 9 sides. Find (a) its exterior angle, (b) its interior angle, (c) the sum of its interior angles.

**(a)** Exterior angle $= 360 ÷ 9 = 40°$.

**(b)** Interior angle $= 180 - 40 = 140°$.

**(c)** Two ways to get the sum:

- Formula: $(9 - 2) × 180 = 7 × 180 = 1260°$
- Or simply $9 × 140 = 1260°$

They agree, which is a good sign.

**Going backwards:** *A regular polygon has an interior angle of 150°. How many sides does it have?*

Exterior angle $= 180 - 150 = 30°$.

Number of sides $= 360 ÷ 30 = 12$.

If this division does not give a whole number, the polygon cannot be regular with that angle, which is sometimes exactly what a "show that" question wants you to explain.

question.text: A regular polygon has 12 sides. Work out the size of one interior angle, in degrees.
question.hint: Find the exterior angle first by dividing 360° by the number of sides.
question.explanation: Exterior angle $= 360 ÷ 12 = 30°$. Interior angle $= 180 - 30 = 150°$. Check with the formula: $(12 - 2) × 180 ÷ 12 = 1800 ÷ 12 = 150°$.

question.text:
Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 156°.

(a) Work out the size of one exterior angle.

(b) Work out the number of sides of the polygon.

(c) Work out the sum of the interior angles of the polygon.
question.hint: Interior and exterior angles at a vertex add to 180°. All the exterior angles add to 360°.

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- Straight line **180°**, around a point **360°**, vertically opposite angles **equal**.
- Parallel lines: **alternate** (Z) equal, **corresponding** (F) equal, **co-interior** (C) add to 180°. Always write the full name as your reason.
- Triangle angles sum to **180°**; quadrilateral angles sum to **360°**. Isosceles triangles have two equal base angles. Exterior angle of a triangle = sum of the two opposite interior angles.
- Polygon interior sum $= (n - 2) × 180°$. Exterior angles of **any** polygon sum to **360°**.
- Regular polygon: exterior $= 360 ÷ n$, interior $= 180 -$ exterior, $n = 360 ÷$ exterior.

practiceQuestions.text: Two angles lie on a straight line. One of them is 63°. Work out the other angle in degrees.
practiceQuestions.hint: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: co-interior angles between parallel lines are always equal.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the C shape. Are the two angles inside it the same size?
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Co-interior angles add up to 180°. It is alternate and corresponding angles that are equal.

options.feedback: Co-interior angles are supplementary: they add up to 180°.

practiceQuestions.text: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5. Work out the size of the largest angle in degrees.
practiceQuestions.hint: Call the angles $3x$, $4x$ and $5x$ and use the fact that they add up to 180°.

practiceQuestions.text: What is the size of each exterior angle of a regular octagon?
practiceQuestions.hint: The exterior angles of any polygon add up to 360°, and a regular octagon has eight equal ones.

options.feedback: That is the interior angle. The exterior angle is 180° minus this.
That is the exterior angle of a regular hexagon.

metadata.blanksText: The interior angles of a polygon with n sides add up to (n − ___) × 180°. The exterior angles of any polygon add up to ___°.

practiceQuestions.hint: A quadrilateral splits into two triangles; a full turn is one complete circle.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Sum of interior angles $= (n - 2) × 180°$ because the polygon splits into $n - 2$ triangles. The exterior angles always add to 360°.

practiceQuestions.text: Put these steps in the correct order to find one interior angle of a regular polygon.
practiceQuestions.hint: You need the exterior angle before you can find the interior angle.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Count the sides, divide 360° by that number to get the exterior angle, subtract from 180° to get the interior angle, then check that the answer is sensible (less than 180° and larger for polygons with more sides).
order: Count the number of sides, n
Divide 360° by n to find one exterior angle
Subtract the exterior angle from 180° to find the interior angle
Check the interior angle is less than 180° and looks sensible

practiceQuestions.text: The four angles of a quadrilateral are $2x + 10$, $x + 30$, $3x − 20$ and $100°$. Work out the value of $x$.
practiceQuestions.hint: The angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360°. Collect the $x$ terms and the numbers separately.

practiceQuestions.text: Select every statement that is true.
practiceQuestions.hint: Work out the actual angles for the pentagon and hexagon rather than guessing.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Exterior angles of any polygon sum to 360° (true). A regular hexagon has exterior angles of 60°, so interior angles of 120° (true). Corresponding angles are equal, not supplementary (false). An equilateral triangle has three 60° angles (true). A regular pentagon has exterior angles of $360 ÷ 5 = 72°$, so 108° is its interior angle (false).

options.text: The exterior angles of any polygon add up to 360°.
Each interior angle of a regular hexagon is 120°.

options.feedback: Corresponding angles are equal. Co-interior angles are the pair that add to 180°.

options.text: Every angle in an equilateral triangle is 60°.
Each exterior angle of a regular pentagon is 108°.
options.feedback: 108° is the interior angle of a regular pentagon; the exterior angle is 72°.

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why the interior angles of a hexagon add up to 720°.
practiceQuestions.hint: Draw diagonals from one corner of the hexagon. How many triangles do you get?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Drawing diagonals from one vertex splits a hexagon into 4 triangles. The angles of each triangle add up to 180°, so the total is $4 × 180 = 720°$.

markScheme.criterion: Splits the hexagon into 4 triangles (from one vertex)

practiceQuestions.text:
The five interior angles of a pentagon are $2x$, $2x$, $x + 40$, $x + 40$ and $100°$.

(a) Write down the sum of the interior angles of a pentagon.

(b) Work out the value of $x$.

(c) Work out the size of the largest angle of the pentagon.
practiceQuestions.hint: Use $(n - 2) × 180°$ with $n = 5$, then form and solve an equation.

practiceQuestions.text: A regular polygon has an exterior angle of 20°. Work out the sum of its interior angles, in degrees.
practiceQuestions.hint: First find the number of sides using $360 ÷$ exterior angle, then use the interior-sum formula.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Number of sides $= 360 ÷ 20 = 18$. Sum of interior angles $= (18 - 2) × 180 = 16 × 180 = 2880°$. Check: each interior angle is $160°$ and $18 × 160 = 2880°$.

practiceQuestions.text: Four angles meet at a point. They are $3k$, $2k + 25$, $k + 35$ and $90°$. Work out the value of $k$.
practiceQuestions.hint: Angles around a point add up to 360°. Add the expressions, collect the $k$ terms and solve.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each angle fact to the correct description.
practiceQuestions.hint: Two of these facts give equal angles and two give a total. Think about where each situation appears in a diagram.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Vertically opposite angles are equal and appear where two straight lines cross. The angles of any quadrilateral add up to 360°. The base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal and sit opposite the equal sides. At any vertex of a polygon the interior and exterior angles lie on a straight line, so they add up to 180°.

pairs.right: Equal – formed where two straight lines cross

pairs.left: Base angles of an isosceles triangle
pairs.right: Equal – opposite the two equal sides

pairs.left: Interior and exterior angle at one vertex of a polygon
pairs.right: Add up to 180° – they lie on a straight line

practiceQuestions.text: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides. One of the angles opposite an equal side is 64°. What is the size of the angle between the two equal sides?
practiceQuestions.hint: There are two base angles, both the same size. Subtract both of them from 180°.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Both base angles are 64°, so the angle between the equal sides is $180 - 64 - 64 = 52°$.

options.feedback: You subtracted only one base angle. There are two of them.
That is the size of the other base angle, not the angle between the equal sides.
Only the base angles are shared equally; the apex angle does not need halving.

practiceQuestions.text: A regular polygon has 20 sides. Work out the size of one interior angle, in degrees.
practiceQuestions.hint: Find the exterior angle first: $360 ÷$ number of sides. Then use the fact that interior and exterior angles add to 180°.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Exterior angle $= 360 ÷ 20 = 18°$. Interior angle $= 180 - 18 = 162°$. Check with the formula: $(20 - 2) × 180 ÷ 20 = 3240 ÷ 20 = 162°$.

practiceQuestions.text:
The outline of a coin is a regular polygon. Each interior angle of the polygon is 165°.

(a) Work out the size of one exterior angle.

(b) Work out the number of sides of the polygon.

(c) Work out the sum of the interior angles of the polygon.
practiceQuestions.hint: Interior and exterior angles at a vertex add to 180°. The exterior angles of any polygon add up to 360°.
